title: TheGreenFeed Deterministic Survey Analysis Framework
purpose: A versioned rules-and-interpretation file for turning aggregate survey responses into transparent findings and practical next steps.

dominance.closeSplit: top two options differ by < 10 percentage points; describe as mixed
dominance.tie: two or more options share the highest count
dominance.smallSampleWarning: For N < 10, show descriptive counts but label interpretation preliminary.

guardrails: Use cautious language: may indicate, is consistent with, suggests.
Never claim causation from this cross-sectional self-report survey.
Do not infer why a student chose an answer unless the survey asked why.
Do not treat missing answers as A, B or C.
Show N and counts alongside percentages; small percentage differences are not automatically meaningful.
Compare related questions before recommending an intervention.
Do not claim respondents represent all PCTE students unless the sampling method supports that.
Separate observed facts from interpretation and recommendations.

rules: Because name and course are collected, do not call responses anonymous.
Keep names and phone numbers out of aggregate analysis and analysis exports.
Raw response export contains identifying data and must be admin-only.
Suppress or combine very small programme groups in breakdowns.

a.label: Rarely or never
a.interpretation: Low reported visibility; could reflect cleaner routes/times or lower exposure.

b.label: Sometimes
b.interpretation: An intermittent or location-specific problem may be present.

c.label: Often or very often
c.interpretation: A visible problem may warrant hotspot checks and direct observation.

a.label: Canteens, food areas or student gathering spots
a.interpretation: Inspect food packaging, peak traffic, bin access and collection frequency.

b.label: Classrooms, corridors or other shared indoor areas
b.interpretation: Review indoor bin access, labels, routines and cleaning schedules.

c.label: Outdoor areas, pathways or other places around campus
c.interpretation: Review outdoor bin placement, high-traffic paths and wind-blown litter.

questions.construct: Stated response when the nearest bin is inconvenient

a.label: Use the nearest bin or leave the waste nearby
a.interpretation: May signal convenience barriers; this option combines two behaviours, so interpret cautiously.

b.label: Look for another bin if one is reasonably close
b.interpretation: Suggests some willingness to make an extra effort when manageable.

c.label: Keep the waste with me until I find a suitable place to dispose of it
c.interpretation: Suggests stated willingness to hold waste until a suitable bin is found.

a.label: Usually ignore it
a.interpretation: Non-intervention is common; the survey does not reveal why.

b.label: Feel uncomfortable but usually say nothing
b.interpretation: May indicate a gap between disapproval and willingness to intervene.

c.label: Politely speak up or encourage them to dispose of it properly
c.interpretation: Suggests openness to respectful peer reminders; intention is not observed behaviour.

a.label: Yes, I knew about both
a.interpretation: Reported awareness, not proof of understanding or effectiveness.

b.label: I knew about one of these, but not the other
b.interpretation: Partial awareness may point to incomplete or unclear communication.

c.label: No, I did not know about either
c.interpretation: May indicate rules are not reaching many respondents.

a.label: I was not aware of these fines before this survey
a.interpretation: Compare with q5; mismatches may reflect recall or interpretation.

b.label: I know about them, but they have little or no influence on my behaviour
b.interpretation: Awareness alone may not be enough; this does not prove enforcement is ineffective.

c.label: They make me more careful about littering or chewing gum on campus
c.interpretation: Reports perceived deterrence, not a causal effect.

questions.construct: Visibility and recall of campus messages

a.label: I rarely or never notice them
a.interpretation: Placement, clutter or salience may be limiting visibility.

b.label: I sometimes notice posters, but rarely remember what they say
b.interpretation: Messages may be seen but not memorable or actionable.

c.label: I notice them and can remember at least one message
c.interpretation: Some messaging is recalled; recall does not prove behaviour change.

a.label: I have not noticed these events or their environmental messages
a.interpretation: Event-based environmental communication may have limited reach.

b.label: I have noticed the event, but do not remember an environmental or waste-management message
b.interpretation: The event may be visible while its environmental message is not salient.

c.label: I remember seeing or hearing an environmental or waste-management message through one of these events
c.interpretation: The message reached the respondent; recall does not prove action.

a.label: Little or none
a.interpretation: May indicate an education or communication gap.

b.label: Some guidance, but not enough to feel consistent or practical
b.interpretation: Guidance may be too abstract, occasional or disconnected from disposal points.

c.label: Enough practical guidance to understand what I should do
c.interpretation: Perceived adequacy should be checked against q10 and actual sorting conditions.

a.label: Not confident; I am unsure how to separate them correctly
a.interpretation: Practical, item-specific guidance may help; confidence is not a test of actual accuracy.

b.label: Somewhat confident, but unsure about at least one item
b.interpretation: Targeted guidance on confusing items may be useful.

c.label: Confident that I know how to separate all three
c.interpretation: High self-reported confidence; actual sorting accuracy remains untested.

a.label: Bins are hard to find, overflowing or not clearly labelled
a.interpretation: Prioritize an infrastructure audit of access, capacity, labels and placement.

b.label: Students lack awareness, motivation or clear guidance
b.interpretation: Test practical guidance and peer-norm interventions while checking infrastructure.

c.label: Both seem manageable to me; neither stands out as the main obstacle
c.interpretation: Other barriers may exist; this does not prove there is no problem.

b.interpretation: Practical education may be preferred over broad awareness messaging.

c.label: Student-led activities that make proper disposal a shared campus habit
c.interpretation: A voluntary peer-led pilot may be worth testing.

b.interpretation: Test well-placed prompts, especially near disposal decisions.

c.label: Live demonstrations, challenges or student events
c.interpretation: Interactive formats may appeal; evaluate access, cost and actual participation.

sectionAnalysis.label: The Reality
sectionAnalysis.purpose: Describe reported visibility, perceived hotspots, stated disposal choices when bins are inconvenient, and peer responses.

patterns.meaning: Frequent reported encounters with improper disposal; pair with q2 to identify perceived hotspots.
actions: Check hotspots directly at different times
Audit bins in the leading area

patterns.when: q3 option a is common and q11 option a is common
patterns.meaning: Answers are consistent with a convenience or infrastructure barrier.
actions: Audit bin access, capacity, placement and labels

patterns.when: q4 options a+b exceed option c
patterns.meaning: More respondents report not intervening than speaking up; reasons are unknown.

cautions: Survey reports are not a campus waste audit.
q2 identifies broad perceived areas, not exact locations.

sectionAnalysis.label: What Reaches You?
sectionAnalysis.purpose: Assess reported awareness, message visibility/recall, practical guidance and sorting confidence.

patterns.when: q5 option c or q7 option a is common
patterns.meaning: Rules or messages may not be reaching or attracting respondents' attention.

patterns.when: q7 option b or q8 option b is common
patterns.meaning: Messages/events may be noticed without the environmental message being retained.
actions: Measure recall, not just number of posters

patterns.when: q9 option a/b and q10 option a/b are common
patterns.meaning: Responses suggest practical guidance or sorting confidence may need strengthening.
actions: Use consistent labels that match the actual campus waste system

patterns.when: q5 option a leads and q6 option b leads
patterns.meaning: Many respondents report awareness but little personal influence from fines; this does not prove policy ineffectiveness.
actions: Pair rule communication with practical guidance and convenient disposal

cautions: Compare q5 and q6 because q6 includes an unaware option.
Awareness and recall do not prove comprehension or behaviour change.

sectionAnalysis.label: Make the Change
sectionAnalysis.purpose: Identify perceived barriers, preferred interventions/channels/messages, everyday supports and stated willingness.

patterns.when: q11 option a and/or q12 option a and q15 option a are prominent
patterns.meaning: Respondents repeatedly prioritize bins, access or labels.

patterns.when: q11 option b and q12 option b are prominent, with q9/q10 uncertainty
patterns.meaning: Responses point toward practical education and guidance.

patterns.when: q12 option c or q15 option c is prominent and q16 option c has meaningful support
patterns.meaning: There may be an opening for a voluntary student-led pilot.

patterns.when: q13 and q14 each have a clear leading option
patterns.meaning: Use preferred channel and message as a pilot hypothesis, not a proven effective combination.
actions: Track reach, recall and outcomes separately

cautions: Preferred intervention is not necessarily the most effective or affordable.
Stated willingness is not actual participation.

dimensions.meaning: How often respondents report seeing problems and which broad areas they name.
Whether convenience, capacity, labels or bin placement recur across answers.
Whether messages are noticed/remembered and practical guidance feels adequate.
Whether peer responses and student-led activity look promising.

synthesisRules.summary: A combined approach may be warranted: make correct disposal convenient and provide clear instructions at the point of disposal.
Test message visibility and clarity before simply producing more posters.
Try a small voluntary student-led pilot; confirm interest through actual sign-ups and attendance.

synthesisRules.when: no rule has enough support or leading options are closely split
synthesisRules.summary: Do not force a single conclusion. Report the split and consider a low-cost combined pilot or further targeted observation.

students.action: Use an appropriate bin where available; when practical, keep waste until a suitable disposal point is found.
students.caveat: Do not place all responsibility on students if bins are inaccessible, full or unclear.

students.action: Use polite, non-confrontational reminders or join voluntary activities.

college.action: Audit placement, capacity, overflow, labels and collection schedules in perceived hotspots.
college.caveat: Validate perceptions with observation before costly changes.

college.action: Provide consistent, item-specific labels and demonstrations that match actual campus waste handling.
signals: q9/q10 options a or b common
college.caveat: Confirm local collection rules before publishing sorting guidance.

college.action: Make current waste rules and penalties accurate, clear and easy to find.

thegreenfeed.action: Pilot one clear message through the leading preferred channel and measure recall.
thegreenfeed.caveat: Preference and recall do not prove behaviour change.

thegreenfeed.action: Run a small voluntary activity and track sign-ups, attendance and feedback.
thegreenfeed.caveat: Do not infer attendance from stated willingness.

thegreenfeed.action: Repeat a short measurement after a pilot and add direct observation where possible.
thegreenfeed.caveat: Without a suitable comparison design, changes cannot be attributed solely to the campaign.

metrics: A/B/C counts and percentages per question

limitations: This is deterministic descriptive analysis, not a validated psychometric instrument or causal model.
The questionnaire only supports interpretations its wording/options reasonably allow; do not invent unasked reasons.
Recall, social desirability, selection bias and uneven participation can affect results.
Respondents are not automatically representative of all PCTE students.
Report what a pattern is consistent with, not what it proves.
Claims of improvement require follow-up measurements and preferably direct observation.
Programme-level comparisons can mislead when group sizes differ or are very small.
